articles.headline_raw:
RBI shores up rupee. It
may be good tolet it be
articles.body_raw:
N WEDNESDAY, the Indian nupee registered its best
gain against theUS dollar in seven months following
an intervention by the Reserve Bank of India. Asare-
sult of the RBI selling dollars, the nipee’s exchange
rate versus the dollar rose by over 1 per cent during the day. By
theclose of day, the rupee had gained 07 per cent over the dollar
andthe exchange rate had shifted from 91.05 toa dollar to 90.09
to a dollar. The RBI’s intervention in the form of amassive sale
of dollars, increasing the relative supply of dollars vis-a-vis the
rupee and boosting the relative price of the rupee, camein the
wake ofasharp fallin the nipee’s exchange rate versusthe dollar.
Beforethis intervention, the rupee had lost more than6 percent
of its value over the past year — almost two to three times the
rate at which the rupee hashistorically lost value relative to the
dollar. The rapidity of this fall was particularly sharpasthe rupee
lost 3 per cent relative to the dollar since November 15.
At one level, the RBI’s intervention is nothing new, and is
understandable. In the mostrecent monetary policyreview on
December 5, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotrasounded sanguine
about the rupee’s exchange rate trajectory ashe delineated the
RBI's approach. “Our stated policy, always, has been that we
allow the markets to determine (the value of rupee). We don’t
target any price levels orany (price) bands... Oureffort always
has been to reduce any abnormal or excessive volatility and
that is what we will continueto endeavour,” he said. There are
no set definitions of what constitutes “excessive” fluctuation,
butit isnoteworthy thatthe mpeeslid from 90 to 91 ina matter
of just10 days. There is always arisk thata sustained sharp fall
turns intoa panic and becomes self-fulfilling.
With India’s domestic inflation being below even the RBI's
com fort zone and with crude oil prices staying subdued, this is
as good a time as any for the RBI to let the rupee depreciate
against the dollar —since a weaker rupee will not result in spik-
ing domestic inflation to uncomfortable levels. RBI interven-
tions can only achieve the goal of moderating fluctuations in
the rupee’s exchange rate. They cannotbe, and should notbe,
the way forward for an economy that is open to trading globally.
Eventually, the rupee’s true value can only be determined by
the ground realities of how much India exports and imports
and how well itattracts global capital flows.

articles.headline_raw:
Insulate Dhaka ties
from short-term politics
articles.body_raw:
HE PROTESTS at Indian diplomatic outposts, includ-
ing the High Commission in Dhaka, are concerning.
They also carry a disquieting portent for a bilateral re-
lationship that was, until recently, arguably Delhi’s
greatest success in the neighbourhood. The demand for the re-
patriation of Sheikh Hasina by the group marching under the
banner of “July Oikya” and the anti-India rhetoric of National
Citizen Party leader Hasnat Abdullah, threatening to provide
shelter and support to separatists from northeastern states, less
than two months before the general elections, show just how
deeply politicised bilateral ties have become. Delhi has sum-
moned the Bangladesh High Commissioner and made its con-
cerns known. However, the leadershin at the highest level in both
Cotintries must prioritise the need to repair the relationship.
With the benefit of hindsight, it is clear that India underesti-
mated the depth of support for thestudent-led uprising and the
anger against Sheikh Hasina. During the protests and in their
aftermath, certain sections on both sides of the border further
polarised the conversation by invoking historical socialand com-
munal fissures in the Subcontinent. In the age of 24/7 news and
WhatsApp forwards, irresponsible rhetoric cannot butaffect the
tenor ofties with animportant neighbour. Onits part, theinterim
government in Dhaka has done little to bridge the domestic
political divide. As Sajeeb Wazed Joy, Sheikh Hasina’s son, under-
lined in an interview to this newspaper, the Awami League has
been a major political force in Bangladesh since its formation,
andthe ban on theparty fromcontesting will castashadowover
the election. By excluding the Awami League from the political
process, theinterim government is repeating Hasina’s mistakes.
It is important for Delhi and Dhaka to recall the realities of
geography, history, culture, geopolitics and economics that can-
not be wished away. Both countries have made strides in trade,
tackling insurgencies, sharing river waters and policing the
shared 4,096-km land border. India must communicate to the
people of Bangladesh as muchas its government that the bilat-
eralstory isaboutiwosocieties, regardiess ofthe government in
power. Delhi must becareful not to takepolitical sidesin Dhaka.
The political class in Bangladesh, foritspart, needsto show ma-
turity ahead oftheelection. Inthe longterm, both countries have
much to gain by building back the relationship.

articles.headline_raw:
Little Foot tells a big
evolution story
articles.body_raw:
NEW study on “Little Foot”, one of the world’s most
complete early human fossils, could reshape the
understanding of human evolution as it stands. First
discovered in 1994-1998 in the cave system of Sterk-
fontein, South Africa, and unveiled to the public in 2017, “Little
Foot” was long thought to be either a member of the Australo-
pithecus prometheus or of the Australopithecus africanus. The
new study, published in the American Journal of Biological An-
thropology, posits that the skeleton belongs to neither family. It
may actually be part of anew species of human ancestorsentirely.
This is the latest addition to the ever-changing picture of
evolution. Initially thought to be linear, evolution is increas-
ingly being seen as a more diffuse process. Just as the dis-
coveries with “Little Foot” point to the existence of another
branch in the human familytree, another discovery earlier this
year challenges the very timeline of human evolution. A skull
discovered by a team of researchers in China was thought to
belong to the Homo erectus, given that it was a million years
old. However, genetic studies on the remnant uncovered that
it likely belonged to Homo longi, aspecies with similar levels of
cerebral development as Homo sapiens and Neanderthals.
That theevolution of Homosapniens —in fact, thespecies’ very
existence —has been shaped by more factors than previously
imagined makes for a richer story, one that should deepen hu-
mans’ appreciation for theirown ability to adapt andsurvive. In
atime ofgreat existential threats — climate change, wars, AI—
this ever-complicating picture of evolution offers both solace
and upliftment. There may be much that humans areupagainst
—but prehistory shows that they are up to the challenge.
